name: Cruyffism (Cruyff's philosophy)
scopeNote: Cruyffism as an idea: attacking football built on possession (the ball as defence: 'you have what the opposition don't, and therefore they can't score'), positional play by spacing and triangles rather than running, technique first (everything with the ball, rondos), short players with good touch, goalkeeper and defenders in the build-up, high compact block, and an academy that teaches one model from the youth sides up. Exemplars: Johan Cruyff as coach of Ajax (technical director from summer 1985, diploma and formal manager role from January 1986 per FourFourTwo, until 1988) and Barcelona (1988 to 1996, the 'Dream Team': Cup Winners' Cup 1989, Copa del Rey 1990, four La Ligas 1991-94, European Cup 1992). Start 1985-07-01 and end 1996-05-18 (Cruyff's departure from Barcelona) are approximate: the appointment day at Barcelona (1988) and the Ajax exit date were NOT verified on a page in this run; the club history page says only 'sacked by Nunez after two seasons without a trophy' (Planet Football) and 'summer of 1988' (Coaches' Voice). Most tactical detail is from retrospectives (Coaches' Voice 2020, FourFourTwo 2013); period quotes are few. Label: 'Cruyffism' was not found in a primary source in this run; sources say 'the Cruyffian cult/style', 'Cruyffians', and FourFourTwo adds 'just don't call it total football'. The 3-4-3 is the Barcelona formation, not the idea: the Ajax side and the later 4-3-3 (after Romario, 1993) show the principles outlast the shape. Disciples recorded from sources: Pep Guardiola (played in the Dream Team, debut 1990/91; coached Barcelona 2008-12 and cited as the heir), Ronald Koeman, Luis Milla, Albert Ferrer, Sergi, Guillermo Amor, Eusebio Sacristan (Barcelona B coach to 2015), Jordi Cruyff (Valencia general manager, quoted on youth contact), Rijkaard (Passion4FM: laid foundation for Guardiola; not read in depth), plus La Masia products Xavi, Iniesta, Messi (Coaches' Voice). Ajax: Bergkamp debut late 1986, Van Basten, Rijkaard, Cup Winners' Cup 1987.
openQuestions: Cruyffism vs Total Football: Coaches' Voice and FourFourTwo describe Barcelona's 3-4-3 as adapted from the 4-3-3 Cruyff played under Michels at Ajax and Holland, and the club history says Cruyff modified tactics 'to incorporate Rinus Michels's total football'. FourFourTwo (2016) says the Dream Team style is Cruyffian but 'just don't call it total football'. Candidate distinction: total football = interchangeable players in fluid positions; Cruyffism = fixed roles in a positional structure (diamond, triangles, full-backs width, false nine) and an academy model. Needs a primary source.

Cruyffism vs positional play: Coaches' Voice says 'the positional football that Cruyff preached' needed players who understood when to approach teammates. Breaking the Lines (2018, tier C) calls positional play 'the language' Guardiola learned. Whether 'juego de posicion' as a codified system (Guardiola's zones, half-spaces, third man) is Cruyff's or Guardiola's/Pep Lijnders-era development is not resolved; Passion4FM (FM blog, tier D) credits Guardiola with merging Cruyff, Sacchi and total football.

Pressing: sources conflict. 90min and Newstalk (tier C) say a 'high press' / 'high intensity pressing'; Coaches' Voice says his teams 'rarely executed a high or intense counter-press' and conceded many goals; FourFourTwo: 'defensive thinking didn't enter Cruyff's mind'. Reading supported by Coaches' Voice: regain through compactness and positioning, not a Guardiola-style counter-press.

Marking: no source read states zonal vs man-marking for Cruyff's teams. Only inference: positions-based defending and a defender pushed forward; Zubizarreta told to decide set-piece defence. Needs a search on marcaje en zona with a named source.

Ajax 1985-88: only the Bergkamp feature and a FourFourTwo biography were read. The claim of a 3-4-3 and high defensive line at Ajax appeared only in a search summary (unverified). The worldofjohancruyff.com page returned 404.
Date of Cruyff's appointment at Barcelona (1988) and exit (1996) and his Ajax start/end are not verified on a read page; check against a second source.

Label origin: 'Dream Team' was borrowed from the 1992 US Olympic basketball team (90min). The term 'Cruyffism' appears in a Medium page title seen only in a search result (not verified). Cruyff's own text 'My Turn' / 'Fútbol. Mi filosofia' not reached.
The Roar statement (three in midfield, 'I am much more defensive than people think') is undated and left verified:false; the first appearance of the Dutch TV clip was not found.

sources.evidence: It was what he called his diamond formation, but the positional football that Cruyff preached was not always easy to understand. It was possible, but only as long as his players shared his own deep understanding of the game – an understanding that enabled them to decide when to approach their teammates, and indeed when not to.

sources.evidence: “He got a blackboard and drew three defenders, four midfielders, two out-and-out wingers and a centre-forward,” recalls Eusebio. “We looked at each other and said: ‘What the hell is this?!’ This was the era of 4-4-2 or 3-5-2. We couldn’t believe how many attackers were in the team, and how few defenders. He single-handedly introduced a new way of playing football in Spain. It was a revolution.” The 3-4-3 – adapted from the 4-3-3 Cruyff played under Rinus Michels for Ajax and Holland in the 1970s – was born.

statedView.quote: It’s a basic concept: when you dominate the ball, you move well. You have what the opposition don’t, and therefore they can’t score. The person that moves decides where the ball goes, and if you move well, you can change opponents’ pressure into your advantage.
If you have four men defending two strikers, you only have six against eight in the middle of the field: there’s no way you can win that battle. We had to put a defender further forward.

I was criticised for playing three at the back, but that’s the most idiotic thing I’ve ever heard. What we needed was to fill the middle of the pitch with players where we needed it most. I much prefer to win 5-4 than 1-0.
Milan are nothing out of this world. They base their game on defence, we base ours on attack.
If you don’t lose the ball in the build-up, it’s very difficult to be counter-attacked.
I am much more defensive than people think.
Football basically consists of two things. First, when you have the ball, you must be able to pass it properly. Second, when the ball is passed to you, you must be able to control it.
